en: Majjhima Nikāya 52:
Aṭṭhakanāgarasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in the village of Beluva.
Now at that time, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara went to the Cock’s Park (Kukkuṭārāma) where a certain bhikkhu was staying.
Having approached and paid homage to that bhikkhu, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said this to that bhikkhu:
"Venerable sir, where is the Venerable Ānanda staying at present?"
“Indeed, we wish to see that venerable Ānanda.
“Householder, that venerable Ānanda is staying at Vesālī in the village of Beluva.
Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara, having finished his business in Pāṭaliputta, went toward Vesālī.
He approached the village of Beluva where the Venerable Ānanda was staying;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Venerable Ānanda, has there not been declared by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One— a single dharma,
wherein for a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute,
the mind that was not yet liberated becomes liberated, the taints that were not yet exhausted reach exhaustion, and that which was not yet attained— the unsurpassed— [is attained]?”
“...does he attain the security from bondage? “Householder,
there is indeed one thing taught by that Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
whereby for a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, [that which was] unliberated...”
“The mind is liberated, the unabandoned taints go to their destruction, and one attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been attained.
“But, venerable Ānanda, what was it that the Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One— [taught]?”
“One dhamma has been taught, wherein for a bhikkhu who dwells heedful,
ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind becomes liberated, the unabandoned taints reach their exhaustion,
and the unsurpassed security from bondage, not yet attained, is reached.”

“Here, householder, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
He reflects thus:
‘This first jhāna, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced.’”
But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced, that is impermanent and subject to cessation—thus he understands.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very passion for the Dhamma and delight in the Dhamma, with the total exhaustion of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, no longer subject to return from that world.
This too, householder, is one thing declared by that Blessed One— who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—
whereby the mind of a bhikkhu who dwells diligent, ardent,
and resolute becomes liberated if it was not yet liberated, and his unabated taints go to their exhaustion, and he attains the unsurpassed state that had not yet been attained.
He attains the security from bondage.
Furthermore, householder, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which possesses internal confidence and...
[as above] ...he reflects thus:
“This second jhāna, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced...
[he] attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Furthermore, householder, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the third jhāna...”
Thus he reflects:
‘This third jhāna, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced...
[he] attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.’
Furthermore, householder, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He reflects thus:
‘This fourth jhāna, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced... [as before].
He attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;
likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as himself, he dwells.
He dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
He reflects thus:
‘This liberation of mind through loving-kindness is conditioned and volitionally produced.
But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation,’ he understands.
Established therein... [as before]...
He attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Furthermore, householder, with a mind imbued with compassion… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy… [and so on]… he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
With a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, everywhere and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus he reflects:
"This liberation of mind through equanimity is also conditioned and volitionally produced.
And whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation. Thus he understands.
Abiding there, he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.

Furthermore, householder, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking “space is infinite,” a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
Thus he reflects:
"This attainment of the base of infinite space is indeed conditioned and volitionally produced.
And whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation. Thus he understands.
Standing there, he...
[and so on] ...attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
Thus he reflects:
"This attainment of the base of infinite consciousness is also conditioned and volitionally produced.
And whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation. Thus he understands.
Established therein, he...
attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Thus he reflects:
"This attainment of the base of nothingness is also conditioned and volitionally produced.
And whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation. Thus he understands.
Established therein, one attains the destruction of the taints.

If one does not attain the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, one becomes of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This too, householder, is a single thing taught by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“Wherein, for a bhikkhu who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute,
the mind that was not yet liberated becomes liberated, the taints that were not yet exhausted go to exhaustion,
and the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not yet been reached is attained.”
When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Just as if, venerable Ānanda, a man seeking one entrance to a hidden treasure were suddenly to find eleven entrances to hidden treasures;
even so, venerable sir, while seeking one door to the Deathless, I have found eleven doors to the Deathless for development.”
“Venerable sir, just as if a man had a house with eleven doors, and that house were on fire, he would be able to effect his own safety through even one single door;
even so, venerable sir, I shall be able to effect my own safety through even one single door among these eleven doors to the Deathless.
Venerable sir, if those belonging to other sects seek the teacher’s fee for their teacher, why then should I not pay honor to the Venerable Ānanda?”
Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara, having assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from Pāṭaliputta and Vesālī, personally satisfied and served them with excellent hard and soft foods;

he presented each bhikkhu individually with a pair of cloths and presented the Venerable Ānanda with a triple robe. He also had a monastery built for the Venerable Ānanda at the cost of five hundred [pieces of gold].
The second discourse, the Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta, is finished.
